p: The koala lives in a gum tree. It eats the leaves and sleeps a lot. Koalas can sleep for most of the day.
A kangaroo has strong back legs. It uses its tail to help it balance. A baby kangaroo is called a joey.
The wombat has a short tail and strong claws. It digs a burrow under the ground. It sleeps there in the day.
We went to the zoo on Saturday. I saw a platypus swim in a tank. It was small and very fast.
Kookaburras sit in tall trees. They make a loud sound like a laugh. You can hear them in the morning.
The echidna has spines on its back. When it is scared, it rolls into a ball. It eats ants with its long tongue.

s: Koalas sleep up to twenty hours a day to save energy.
The platypus is one of the few mammals that lay eggs.
A wombat's droppings are shaped like little cubes.
Red kangaroos can jump more than eight metres in one bound.
Little penguins return to the beach at dusk in Victoria.
Echidnas use their long sticky tongues to catch termites.
The Tasmanian devil makes a loud and scary screech at night.
Many Australian birds build nests in hollow tree branches.
Green sea turtles travel thousands of kilometres across the ocean.
The cassowary has a tall helmet called a casque on its head.
Flying foxes help spread seeds when they fly between trees.
A male emu sits on the eggs until the chicks hatch.
Sugar gliders can glide between trees using flaps of skin.
The thorny devil collects water through grooves in its skin.
Humpback whales swim north along the coast every winter.
Numbats eat thousands of termites every single day.
Some frogs in the desert stay underground until it rains.
The lyrebird can copy the sounds of cameras and chainsaws.
Crocodiles in northern Australia can grow over five metres long.
A blue-tongue lizard shows its tongue to scare away danger.
Rainbow lorikeets drink nectar from flowers with brush-like tongues.
Dugongs graze on seagrass in warm, shallow water.
Bilbies dig spiral burrows to stay cool in the desert.
The kookaburra is the largest member of the kingfisher family.
Wildlife carers look after animals that have been hurt.
p: Koalas are marsupials, which means their babies grow in a pouch. A newborn koala is about the size of a jellybean. It stays in the pouch for around six months before it climbs onto its mother's back.

The platypus is a very unusual animal. It has a bill like a duck, a tail like a beaver and webbed feet. It hunts for food at the bottom of rivers with its eyes closed, finding prey with special sensors in its bill.

Wombats are strong diggers with short, powerful legs. They make long tunnels and rooms under the ground. During a bushfire, other animals have been seen sheltering in wombat burrows to stay safe from the flames.

Every year, little penguins come ashore on Phillip Island at sunset. Visitors sit quietly and watch them waddle up the beach to their burrows. Cameras and torches are not allowed because bright lights can scare the birds.

The echidna is covered in sharp spines that protect it from danger. When it feels threatened, it digs into the soil or curls into a spiky ball. Like the platypus, the echidna is a mammal that lays eggs.
Flying foxes are large bats that eat fruit and nectar. They travel long distances at night looking for food. As they move from tree to tree, they carry pollen and seeds, which helps new forests grow.

s: Koalas have a special gut bacteria that helps them digest the tough, toxic leaves of eucalyptus trees.
Because the platypus lays eggs, scientists call it a monotreme, a group shared only with echidnas.
Habitat loss from land clearing is one of the biggest threats facing Australian wildlife today.
The cane toad was brought to Queensland in 1935 and quickly became a serious invasive species.
Wildlife corridors allow animals to move safely between patches of bushland that have been divided by roads.
Many native animals are nocturnal, so they rest during the hot day and search for food at night.
The Great Barrier Reef is home to thousands of species of fish, coral, turtles and sharks.
Volunteers count birds every spring to help researchers understand how populations are changing.
Bushfires can destroy food and shelter, but some plants actually need fire to release their seeds.
The Tasmanian devil population has dropped sharply because of a contagious facial tumour disease.
A lyrebird's song can contain the calls of more than twenty other bird species.
Saltwater crocodiles can live in both fresh and salty water and may travel far out to sea.
Feral cats and foxes hunt many small native mammals that evolved without these predators.
Rangers use motion-sensing cameras to record which animals visit a waterhole at night.
The bilby has become a symbol of conservation, especially as an Easter alternative to the rabbit.
Some lizards can drop their tails to escape a predator and later grow a new one.
Marine turtles return to the same beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
Desert animals survive with very little water by getting moisture from the food they eat.
Scientists fit tiny tracking devices to birds to learn where they travel during migration.
The southern cassowary plays an important role by spreading the seeds of rainforest fruit.
Australia has more species of venomous snakes than any other continent, yet bites are rare.
A food web shows how energy passes from plants to plant-eaters and then to predators.
Platypuses close their eyes, ears and nostrils underwater and rely on electroreception to hunt.
Breeding programs at zoos help increase the numbers of endangered species such as the corroboree frog.
Many farmers now leave strips of native vegetation to give wildlife food and shelter.
p: Australia is home to many animals found nowhere else on Earth. Because the continent was isolated for millions of years, its wildlife developed in unique ways. Marsupials such as kangaroos and koalas became common, while monotremes like the platypus and echidna survived as rare egg-laying mammals. This makes Australian ecosystems especially valuable to scientists studying evolution.

Invasive species can cause enormous damage to native wildlife. Rabbits compete with native animals for food and dig up the soil, while foxes and feral cats hunt small mammals and birds. Controlling these pests is difficult and expensive, but projects such as predator-proof fences have helped some threatened species recover inside protected areas.

The koala faces several serious threats. Land clearing removes the trees it needs for food and shelter, and roads and dogs put it in danger when it moves across open ground. Disease and heatwaves also take a toll. Planting new eucalyptus trees and protecting existing bushland are two of the most effective ways communities can help.

Marine turtles have survived for millions of years, but they now face new dangers. Plastic bags can look like jellyfish, so turtles sometimes swallow them by mistake. Bright lights near beaches can confuse hatchlings, leading them away from the ocean. Many coastal towns now reduce lighting during nesting season to give baby turtles a better chance.

Ecologists often describe the dingo as an apex predator, meaning it sits at the top of the food chain. Some research suggests dingoes help control the numbers of foxes and kangaroos, which can protect plants and smaller animals. However, dingoes can also attack livestock, so farmers and scientists continue to debate how they should be managed.

Citizen science projects allow ordinary people to contribute to real research. Students can record frog calls on a smartphone app, photograph birds in their backyard or count insects in the school garden. When thousands of observations are combined, scientists gain a much clearer picture of where species live and how they respond to changes in their environment.

s: Australia's long geographic isolation produced an extraordinary level of endemism, with most of its mammals found nowhere else on the planet.
Conservation biologists argue that protecting entire ecosystems is more effective than focusing on a single charismatic species.
The extinction of the thylacine in the twentieth century remains a powerful warning about the consequences of persecution and habitat loss.
Climate change is shifting the ranges of many species southward or to higher altitudes as they seek cooler conditions.
Indigenous rangers combine traditional ecological knowledge with modern technology to manage fire and monitor threatened wildlife.
Biological control has a mixed history in Australia, ranging from the success of myxomatosis to the disaster of the cane toad.
Coral bleaching occurs when rising water temperatures cause corals to expel the algae that supply most of their energy.
Genetic diversity allows a population to adapt to new diseases and environmental pressures, which is why small populations are so vulnerable.
Researchers are investigating whether detection dogs can locate koalas in dense forest more efficiently than human surveys.
The concept of a keystone species describes an organism whose influence on its ecosystem is far greater than its numbers suggest.
Fragmented habitats create edge effects, where conditions such as light, wind and predation change along the borders of remaining bush.
Rewilding projects aim to restore ecological processes by reintroducing species that have disappeared from a landscape.
Some ecologists question whether intensive captive breeding can succeed if the original threats in the wild are never addressed.
Long-term monitoring data is essential because short studies can easily mistake natural fluctuations for permanent trends.
The platypus is listed as near threatened, partly because drought and dams have reduced the flow of many eastern rivers.
Urban wildlife such as possums and brush turkeys show how some species adapt successfully to living alongside people.
Environmental DNA sampling allows scientists to detect rare aquatic animals simply by analysing traces left in a sample of water.
Biodiversity offsets, which compensate for habitat destroyed in one place by protecting land elsewhere, remain highly controversial.
The migratory journeys of shorebirds link Australian wetlands to breeding grounds in the Arctic, thousands of kilometres away.
Protecting a species legally means little unless governments also provide funding for recovery plans and their enforcement.
Predator-free sanctuaries have allowed animals such as the bilby and burrowing bettong to recover in parts of their former range.
Heat stress during extreme summers has caused mass deaths of flying foxes, revealing how vulnerable some species are to warming.
Scientists use stable isotope analysis of feathers and fur to reconstruct the diets of animals over many months.
Community engagement is often the deciding factor in whether a local conservation project survives beyond its first few years.
Understanding animal behaviour can inform smarter road design, such as underpasses that allow wildlife to cross highways safely.
p: Australia has one of the worst records of mammal extinction in the modern world. Since European settlement, more than thirty native mammal species have disappeared, most of them small ground-dwelling marsupials and rodents. Scientists generally attribute these losses to a combination of introduced predators, altered fire regimes and widespread land clearing. Understanding why particular species were vulnerable helps conservationists predict which animals are most at risk today and where limited resources should be directed.

Traditional fire management practised by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples for tens of thousands of years created a patchwork of burnt and unburnt land. These cool, carefully timed burns reduced fuel loads and provided a variety of habitats for wildlife. Following colonisation, many of these practices were interrupted, and some researchers link the resulting changes in fire patterns to declines in certain species. Today, cultural burning programs are being revived in partnership with land management agencies.

The story of the cane toad illustrates the risks of introducing a species without fully understanding its effects. Released to control beetles in sugar cane crops, the toad failed at that task but spread rapidly across northern Australia. Its toxic skin kills many predators that try to eat it, including quolls, goannas and freshwater crocodiles. Some researchers are now training predators to avoid toads through taste aversion, an approach that shows promising early results.

Coral reefs are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems on Earth, yet they occupy a tiny fraction of the ocean floor. The Great Barrier Reef supports fishing and tourism industries worth billions of dollars, as well as countless species. Repeated marine heatwaves have caused widespread bleaching, and although corals can recover, the time between events is becoming shorter. Scientists warn that the long-term health of the reef depends largely on reducing global greenhouse gas emissions.

Debate continues over how to manage large populations of kangaroos in some regions. During good seasons their numbers can rise sharply, leading to overgrazing and, in drought, mass starvation. Some argue that regulated harvesting is a humane and sustainable solution, while others prefer non-lethal methods such as fertility control. The disagreement reflects deeper questions about the relationship between people, agriculture and native wildlife in a changing landscape.

Citizen science has transformed the way information about Australian wildlife is collected. Platforms that allow the public to upload photographs and sound recordings now hold millions of verified observations. These records have helped scientists discover range extensions, track the spread of invasive species and even identify new populations of animals once thought to be locally extinct. However, data from volunteers can be uneven, so researchers must carefully account for where and when people tend to look.
